name: Imperialism
summary: Imperialism as an advocated doctrine holds that a strong nation should extend its rule and influence over other lands and peoples. Its late nineteenth-century defenders argued that empire secured markets, jobs and naval bases, kept a nation in the first rank of powers, and was a duty of 'higher' or 'governing' races to bring order, an end to slavery and civilisation to peoples they judged unfit to govern themselves. Many also hoped to bind the mother country and its settler colonies, or the whole English-speaking world, into one federation.
scope: The pro-imperialist doctrine of the 'new imperialism', roughly 1870 to 1922, as argued by its advocates: Disraeli's Crystal Palace speech, Dilke's Greater Britain, Seeley's Expansion of England, Ferry's 1884 speech, Chamberlain's speeches, Rhodes's will and aims, Kidd's Control of the Tropics, Mahan on sea power, Beveridge's March of the Flag, Kipling's White Man's Burden and Lugard's Dual Mandate. It excludes the practice of empire as such, ancient empires, the Hobson-Lenin critique and modern informal senses of the term. Its thinkers wrote mainly on foreign, colonial and racial questions, so most domestic and modern answers are low-confidence inferences.

furtherReading.title: Jules Ferry on French Colonial Expansion (1884)
furtherReading.note: A short speech that sets out the economic, strategic and civilising-duty arguments in one place.

furtherReading.title: Joseph Chamberlain, The True Conception of Empire (1897)
furtherReading.note: The British case for empire as trusteeship, in the Colonial Secretary's own words.

furtherReading.title: Colonialism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
furtherReading.note: How philosophers from Vitoria to Mill justified colonial rule, and how it was criticised.

furtherReading.title: New Imperialism (Wikipedia)
furtherReading.note: Overview of the period's motives, from social Darwinism to markets and missions.

sources.title: Speech before the French Chamber of Deputies, 28 March 1884
sources.author: Jules Ferry (Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
sources.usedFor: Markets, coaling stations, the duty of higher races to civilise lower ones, national greatness versus decadence.

sources.title: The White Man's Burden (1899)
sources.author: Rudyard Kipling (Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
sources.usedFor: Imperial rule as a thankless duty: famine relief, ending disease, governing resentful peoples.

sources.title: The True Conception of Empire (speech to the Royal Colonial Institute, 31 March 1897)
sources.author: Joseph Chamberlain (Wikisource)
sources.usedFor: Trusteeship, the 'governing race', acceptance of force and bloodshed, settler colonies as kin and partners, hope of federation.

sources.title: The Doctrine of Commercial Imperialism (Birmingham speech, 1893)
sources.author: Joseph Chamberlain (Vancouver Island University course reader)
sources.usedFor: Empire as markets and employment for British workers; attack on Little Englanders; stronger navy.

sources.title: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922)
sources.author: Frederick Lugard (Internet Archive)
sources.usedFor: Dual mandate, open door, abolition of slavery, indirect rule through chiefs, views of the educated African and of 'child races'.

sources.title: The Last Will and Testament of Cecil John Rhodes, with Elucidatory Notes (1902)
sources.author: W. T. Stead (ed.) (Internet Archive)
sources.usedFor: Rhodes's aims: unity of the English-speaking race, recovery of the United States, a secret society, federation, free trade with differential rates.

sources.title: The Control of the Tropics (1898)
sources.author: Benjamin Kidd (Internet Archive)
sources.usedFor: Tropics as a trust for civilisation; native incapacity for self-rule; no white settlement; open markets; rejection of withdrawal.

sources.title: The March of the Flag (16 September 1898)
sources.author: Albert J. Beveridge (Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
sources.usedFor: Providential mission, consent limited to those capable of self-government, markets, naval bases, free trade within the empire.

sources.title: The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890), extract
sources.author: Alfred Thayer Mahan (Vancouver Island University course reader)
sources.usedFor: Navy proportionate to commerce, colonies and stations abroad, naval superiority, government's role in fostering sea power.

sources.title: Greater Britain: A Record of Travel in English-Speaking Countries (1868)
sources.author: Charles Wentworth Dilke (Project Gutenberg)
sources.usedFor: Saxondom: the English-speaking race and its institutions spreading over the globe.

sources.title: The Edwardian assault on free trade
sources.author: Engelsberg Ideas
sources.usedFor: Chamberlain's Tariff Reform: imperial preference, food taxes, revenue for social reform; free-trade opponents.

sources.title: Imperialism (1914-1918-online, International Encyclopedia of the First World War)
sources.author: 1914-1918-online
sources.usedFor: Defining account of the imperialism of the 1880s onward, its civilizing-mission ideology and its navalist and expansionist politicians

notes: Themes searched in the saved texts (Ferry, Chamberlain 1893 and 1897, Disraeli, Beveridge, Mahan, Kipling, Dilke, Seeley's circle, Rhodes's will, Kidd, Lugard): government and law, the world and war, society and race, economy and trade, religion, liberty. The doctrine is about foreign, colonial and racial questions, so most economic, ecological, family and technology statements have no stated position and stay null. Imperialists split on trade (Kidd, Lugard and Rhodes for the open door; Chamberlain's tariff reformers for imperial preference) and on whether colonies existed for metropolitan profit or as a trust. The rules-7 pass nulled earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia, on 'adherents would think' guesses or on one part of a statement. Added from Lugard: religious neutrality of the colonial government and rule through native courts applying native law and custom. Class, secularism-versus-theocracy and several other dividing lines stay uncovered because the imperialists wrote little on them.
